claims.text: Cu-Zr metallic alloys can have their glass-forming ability enhanced through optimization of composition and processing conditions.
A combined experimental and molecular-dynamics simulation approach can identify optimal glass-forming compositions and processing conditions for Cu-Zr alloys.
The initial material is an amorphous, unoptimized Cu-Zr alloy.
A cooling rate of 10^5 K/s is used in the proposed optimization.
The relevant processing temperature range is 500–1000 K.
Short-range order and atomic packing efficiency mediate the glass-forming response.
Optimizing Cu-Zr composition and processing conditions suppresses the nucleation of crystalline phases.
Optimizing Cu-Zr composition and processing conditions suppresses the growth of crystalline phases.
Suppression of crystalline nucleation and growth increases the glass-forming ability of the alloy.
Molecular-dynamics simulations support the proposed crystallization-suppression mechanism.
The optimized Cu-Zr alloy will exhibit a 20% increase in glass-forming ability.
The increase in glass-forming ability can be measured using the critical cooling rate.
Traditional crystalline materials have limited glass-forming ability.
Crystallization is likely at cooling rates below 10^4 K/s.
The optimal composition and processing conditions may depend on the specific alloy system and experimental conditions.
The hypothesis is falsified if the measured glass-forming ability is less than 10% higher than that of traditional crystalline materials.
